hook: The court official honoured for giving the world paper.

pages.x: Cai Lun was a eunuch at the Han court in Luoyang, where he rose to run the workshop that made weapons and tools for the emperor. Books were then written on heavy bundles of bamboo strips, or on silk, which was very costly.
In AD 105 he showed the emperor a writing material made by pounding tree bark, hemp, old rags and fishing nets into pulp, spreading it on a screen and drying it.
pages.fx: Paper was cheap, light and easy to make. It reached the Islamic world in the 700s and Europe in the 1100s, and made printed books and newspapers possible.

pages.x: Archaeologists have found scraps of paper in China from 200 years before him, one with a map drawn on it. He did not invent paper from nothing, but he improved the method, and the court took it up, so the honour went to him.

Cai Lun rose high at court, but years before he had joined a plot against the grandmother of a later emperor. When that emperor took power in 121, he summoned Cai Lun to prison. Instead, Cai Lun bathed, put on his finest robes and drank poison.

A famous story says that after the Battle of Talas in 751, Chinese prisoners taught their Arab captors to make paper in Samarkand. Paper mills soon spread to Baghdad, Cairo and Muslim Spain, and from there into Europe.
Paper is one of the Four Great Inventions of China, and for 2,000 years it has carried the world's knowledge, money and letters. Cai Lun is still honoured as its father.
pts: Allowed books and learning to spread across the world
One of the Four Great Inventions of China
